words.shortDefinition: Fully managed racks of cloud hardware installed in your own data center to run cloud services locally.
words.simpleDefinition: AWS ships, installs, and operates physical racks on your premises so you run the same services and APIs locally — for low latency or data-residency needs — while AWS manages the hardware. It is a true hybrid extension of the cloud into your building. Two form factors exist: full racks and small servers.
words.longDefinition: AWS Outposts extends AWS infrastructure, services, APIs, and tools into on-premises and edge locations as fully managed hardware that AWS delivers, installs, monitors, and maintains. Available as 42U racks or smaller 1U/2U servers, Outposts run a consistent subset of AWS services locally (EC2, EBS, S3 on Outposts, ECS/EKS, RDS, and more), connected back to a parent Region for control-plane operations. It targets workloads needing single-digit-millisecond latency to on-prem systems, local data processing, or data-residency compliance, while preserving the same operational model as the cloud. It contrasts with Local Zones and Wavelength (AWS-owned edge sites) by living inside the customer's own facility.
words.connector: Like a fully-staffed cloud mini-branch installed in your basement: same services and rules as headquarters, but physically next to your factory floor.
words.techContext: The factory's latency-critical control app runs on EC2 on an AWS Outposts rack on the plant floor, syncing to us-east-1.
words.exampleSentence: Regulators required the data to stay on-site, so we ran the database on AWS Outposts instead of the public Region.

codeExample.code:
# List Outposts associated with the account
aws outposts list-outposts \
  --query 'Outposts[].{Name:Name,Site:SiteId,AZ:AvailabilityZone}'

words.etymology: From 'outpost' (a remote station of a larger organization); AWS service launched in 2019.

words.shortDefinition: AWS infrastructure placed in major metro areas to deliver single-digit-millisecond latency to nearby users.
words.simpleDefinition: These are small AWS deployments in big cities, separate from full Regions, that put compute and storage physically close to end users in that metro. You use them for latency-sensitive apps like gaming, media, or real-time rendering. They connect back to a parent Region for the rest of AWS.
words.longDefinition: AWS Local Zones are extensions of an AWS Region placed in or near large population and industry centers, bringing select services (EC2, EBS, ECS, EKS, load balancing, and more) geographically closer to end users than the parent Region allows. They deliver very low latency (often single-digit milliseconds) for applications such as real-time gaming, live video streaming, AR/VR, media production, and machine-learning inference at the metro edge, while non-latency-critical components remain in the parent Region. Unlike Outposts (in the customer's facility) or Wavelength (embedded in telco 5G networks), Local Zones are AWS-owned metro sites you access like any other Availability Zone after enabling them.
words.connector: Like a major retailer opening small downtown branches so city customers get same-hour delivery instead of waiting on the distant regional warehouse.
words.techContext: The cloud-gaming service renders frames in a Los Angeles Local Zone so nearby players see under-10ms latency.
words.exampleSentence: Enabling a Local Zone in the metro dropped interactive latency for those users below the threshold the game needed.

codeExample.code:
# Show opt-in Local Zones available to the account
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --all-availability-zones \
  --filters Name=zone-type,Values=local-zone --query 'AvailabilityZones[].ZoneName'

words.etymology: From 'local' (nearby) + 'zone' (an AZ-like deployment); introduced by AWS in 2019.

words.shortDefinition: Cloud compute embedded inside telecom 5G networks to serve ultra-low-latency mobile-edge applications.
words.simpleDefinition: It places AWS compute and storage at the edge of carriers' 5G networks, so traffic from mobile devices reaches your app without leaving the telecom network. This shaves latency for use cases like AR, connected vehicles, and live video. It is AWS at the mobile edge.
words.longDefinition: AWS Wavelength embeds AWS compute and storage within communications service providers' 5G networks at the edge, in 'Wavelength Zones,' so application traffic from mobile devices can reach servers without traversing the public internet or hopping back to a Region. By terminating at the carrier edge, it minimizes latency for use cases like real-time gaming, AR/VR, autonomous and connected vehicles, live video processing, and industrial automation over 5G. Developers deploy the same EC2/EBS/container resources into a Wavelength Zone tied to a parent Region. It complements Local Zones (metro edge) and Outposts (on-prem) by specifically targeting the mobile-network edge.
words.connector: Like putting a vending machine inside the stadium instead of across town: phones grab what they need right at the network's edge, no long round-trip.
words.techContext: The AR navigation app runs inference in an AWS Wavelength Zone so 5G users get responses in a few milliseconds.
words.exampleSentence: Connected-vehicle telemetry processes in AWS Wavelength at the carrier edge rather than crossing the internet to a Region.

codeExample.code:
# List Wavelength Zones available to the account
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --all-availability-zones \
  --filters Name=zone-type,Values=wavelength-zone --query 'AvailabilityZones[].ZoneName'

words.etymology: From 'wavelength' (radio-spectrum term), nodding to its placement in wireless carrier networks; launched 2019.

words.shortDefinition: The hardware and lightweight hypervisor platform underpinning modern virtual-server instances for performance and security.
words.simpleDefinition: It is the foundation beneath recent EC2 instances: dedicated hardware cards offload networking, storage, and security from the main CPU, and a minimal hypervisor gives nearly bare-metal performance with strong isolation. It is why newer instances are faster and more secure. Customers don't interact with it directly — it just powers EC2.
words.longDefinition: The AWS Nitro System is the underlying platform for modern EC2 instances, built from three parts: Nitro Cards that offload and accelerate VPC networking, EBS storage, and local I/O onto dedicated hardware; the Nitro Security Chip that integrates into the motherboard to lock down hardware and protect firmware; and the lightweight Nitro Hypervisor that provides CPU and memory isolation with minimal overhead, delivering performance close to bare metal. By moving virtualization functions off the main server CPU, Nitro frees nearly all host resources for customer workloads, improves security (AWS operators have no ability to access customer data, validated by the NCC Group), and enables fast innovation in instance types, including bare-metal and Graviton-based options. It is invisible infrastructure that customers benefit from automatically.
words.connector: Like a car where power steering, braking, and security each have their own dedicated module instead of taxing the engine — the engine just drives, fast.
words.techContext: The Nitro System lets our network-heavy instances push high throughput because packet processing runs on dedicated cards, not the vCPUs.
words.exampleSentence: Bare-metal EC2 exists only because the Nitro System moved virtualization off the host CPU entirely.

codeExample.code:
Nitro = Nitro Cards (offload net/storage)
      + Nitro Security Chip (firmware/hardware integrity)
      + Nitro Hypervisor (minimal, near bare-metal isolation)

words.etymology: From 'nitro' (nitrous oxide, slang for a performance boost); AWS introduced the architecture in 2017.

words.shortDefinition: A family of Arm-based processors designed in-house to give better price-performance for cloud workloads.
words.simpleDefinition: These are AWS's own Arm CPUs that power many EC2 instance types, typically offering better performance per dollar and lower energy use than comparable x86. Many workloads run on them with just a recompile. Choosing them is a common cost-and-efficiency win.
words.longDefinition: AWS Graviton is a series of 64-bit Arm-based processors custom-designed by AWS (built on the Nitro System) to deliver superior price-performance and energy efficiency for cloud workloads. Successive generations (Graviton2, Graviton3, Graviton4) power EC2 instance families denoted with a 'g' (e.g., m7g, c7g, r8g) and back managed services like Aurora, RDS, ElastiCache, Lambda, and Fargate. Because most modern languages and container images support Arm, many applications migrate with a rebuild or multi-arch image, gaining roughly 20–40% better price-performance and reduced carbon footprint. Graviton is central to AWS cost-optimization guidance and to its sustainability story, exemplifying vertical integration of silicon for the cloud.
words.connector: Like switching a delivery fleet to efficient engines designed for exactly your routes: same deliveries, noticeably lower fuel bills.
words.techContext: Rebuilding the service as a multi-arch image let us run it on Graviton instances and cut compute cost about 30%.
words.exampleSentence: Moving the Lambda functions to AWS Graviton improved price-performance with no code changes beyond the runtime setting.

codeExample.code:
# Launch a Graviton (arm64) instance
aws ec2 run-instances --instance-type c7g.large \
  --image-id ami-0arm64example --count 1

words.etymology: From 'graviton' (the hypothetical particle mediating gravity); AWS's silicon brand since 2018.

words.shortDefinition: Isolated compute environments carved from an instance for processing highly sensitive data with no persistent storage or external network.
words.simpleDefinition: They let you split off a hardened, fully isolated mini-environment from an EC2 instance — no disk, no network, no operator access — to handle secrets like keys or PII. The parent instance can't peek inside, and cryptographic attestation proves what's running. It is for the most sensitive in-memory processing.
words.longDefinition: AWS Nitro Enclaves are isolated, hardened virtual machines created from a parent EC2 instance's CPU and memory, built on the Nitro System, designed to process highly sensitive data. An enclave has no persistent storage, no interactive access, and no external networking — it communicates with the parent only over a secure local channel (vsock). Cryptographic attestation produces a signed document proving the enclave's identity and measurements, which services like AWS KMS can require before releasing keys, ensuring secrets are only used by verified code. Typical uses include processing PII, financial data, healthcare records, and private keys, and multi-party computation. Enclaves reduce the attack surface so that even a compromised parent instance or privileged operator cannot read the protected data.
words.connector: Like a sealed glovebox inside a lab: hands work the material through it, but nothing — not even the lab owner — can reach in or take anything out.
words.techContext: The signing service runs inside a Nitro Enclave, and KMS only releases the key after verifying the enclave's attestation.
words.exampleSentence: We isolated card decryption in a Nitro Enclave so even root on the host can't read the plaintext.

codeExample.code:
# Run a built enclave image file with allocated resources
nitro-cli run-enclave --eif-path app.eif \
  --cpu-count 2 --memory 512 --enclave-cid 16

words.etymology: From 'enclave' (an enclosed, separate territory), built on the Nitro System; launched 2020.

words.shortDefinition: A managed service offering access to multiple foundation models through one API for building generative-AI applications.
words.simpleDefinition: It gives you a single API to call leading foundation models from several providers (Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, and more) without managing infrastructure. You can customize models, add retrieval and guardrails, and build agents. It is the front door to generative AI on AWS.
words.longDefinition: Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that provides access to a choice of high-performing foundation models (FMs) from providers such as Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, Cohere, Stability AI, and Amazon (Titan/Nova) through a single serverless API. Beyond raw inference, it offers fine-tuning and continued pre-training, Knowledge Bases for retrieval-augmented generation, Agents for multi-step tool-using workflows, Guardrails for safety and content filtering, and model evaluation. Data stays within the customer's control and is not used to train base models. By abstracting infrastructure and unifying model access, Bedrock lets teams build, customize, and scale generative-AI applications — chat, summarization, RAG, agents — while easily swapping models as needs and the model landscape evolve.
words.connector: Like a streaming service for AI brains: one subscription and remote control gives you many top models to summon, swap, and combine without owning the hardware.
words.techContext: The support assistant calls Claude through Amazon Bedrock with a Knowledge Base for RAG and Guardrails for safety.
words.exampleSentence: We prototyped on one model and switched to a stronger one in Amazon Bedrock by changing a single model ID.

codeExample.code:
# Invoke a model through the Bedrock runtime
aws bedrock-runtime invoke-model --model-id anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet \
  --body '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}]}' out.json

words.etymology: From 'bedrock' (the solid rock foundation beneath soil), a base to build upon; AWS service launched in 2023.

words.shortDefinition: An end-to-end platform to build, train, tune, deploy, and manage machine-learning models at scale.
words.simpleDefinition: It covers the whole ML lifecycle: notebooks for development, managed training jobs, hyperparameter tuning, model hosting for inference, and pipelines to automate it all. It removes the heavy lifting of provisioning ML infrastructure. The newer unified studio also folds in analytics and generative AI.
words.longDefinition: Amazon SageMaker is a comprehensive machine-learning platform spanning the full lifecycle: data labeling and preparation (Ground Truth, Data Wrangler), development (Studio notebooks), managed and distributed training with automatic model tuning, experiment tracking, a model registry, and one-click deployment to real-time, serverless, asynchronous, or batch inference endpoints with autoscaling and monitoring (Model Monitor, Clarify for bias/explainability). Pipelines provide CI/CD-style MLOps orchestration, and JumpStart offers prebuilt models and solutions. AWS has been unifying these capabilities with data and analytics in the next-generation SageMaker (with SageMaker Unified Studio). It targets data-science and ML-engineering teams that need to operationalize custom models at scale, complementing Bedrock's focus on consuming foundation models.
words.connector: Like a fully-equipped workshop for building machines: raw materials in one bay, assembly line in another, quality control and shipping at the end — all under one roof.
words.techContext: The recommendation model trains on a SageMaker distributed job and serves from an autoscaling SageMaker endpoint.
words.exampleSentence: We moved the ML pipeline into Amazon SageMaker so training, tuning, and deployment run as one automated workflow.

codeExample.code:
import sagemaker
from sagemaker.estimator import Estimator

est = Estimator(image_uri=img, role=role,
    instance_type="ml.g5.xlarge", instance_count=1)
est.fit({"train": "s3://bucket/train/"})

words.etymology: A blend of 'sage' (a wise person) + 'maker' (one who creates); AWS service launched in 2017.

words.shortDefinition: A generative-AI assistant for developers and businesses that answers questions and acts across code and AWS resources.
words.simpleDefinition: It is AWS's AI assistant: Q Developer helps write, debug, and modernize code and reason about your AWS account, while Q Business answers questions over your company's internal data. It connects to your context rather than being a generic chatbot. It shows up in IDEs, the console, and chat tools.
words.longDefinition: Amazon Q is AWS's family of generative-AI assistants. Amazon Q Developer assists across the software lifecycle — code completion and generation in the IDE, debugging, unit-test and documentation generation, security scanning, large-scale code transformations (e.g., Java version upgrades), and answering questions about your AWS account, costs, and resources. Amazon Q Business is an enterprise assistant that connects to internal data sources (S3, SharePoint, Salesforce, and many connectors) with respect for existing access permissions, enabling employees to ask natural-language questions, summarize, and automate over company knowledge. Grounded in customer context rather than acting as a generic model, Q is surfaced in IDEs, the AWS console, CLI, and collaboration tools, and is built on Amazon Bedrock models.
words.connector: Like a knowledgeable colleague who has read both your codebase and your company wiki, and can either pair-program or answer 'where's that policy?' on demand.
words.techContext: Developers use Amazon Q Developer in the IDE to generate tests and to run a managed Java 8-to-17 code transformation.
words.exampleSentence: Amazon Q answered 'which instances are idle this month?' directly from our account instead of us writing a Cost Explorer query.

codeExample.code:
# Amazon Q Developer in the CLI (after `q login`)
q chat "Explain why this Lambda is timing out and suggest a fix"

words.etymology: The single-letter name 'Q' evokes a helpful, all-knowing assistant; AWS launched it in 2023.

words.shortDefinition: Custom silicon purpose-built to accelerate the training of large machine-learning models at lower cost.
words.simpleDefinition: It is an AWS-designed chip optimized for training big models, powering specialized EC2 instances that aim to train faster and cheaper than general GPUs. You use it through ML frameworks via the Neuron SDK. It targets the heaviest training jobs, like large language models.
words.longDefinition: AWS Trainium is a family of machine-learning accelerator chips designed by AWS specifically for high-performance, cost-efficient training of deep-learning models, including large language and generative-AI models. Trainium powers Trn-series EC2 instances (e.g., trn1, trn2) that scale to large clusters with high-bandwidth interconnect (NeuronLink) and EFA networking for distributed training. Developers target it through the AWS Neuron SDK, which integrates with PyTorch and JAX so models run with minimal code change. Trainium aims to deliver substantially better price-performance than comparable GPU instances for large-scale training, and pairs with Inferentia (its inference-optimized counterpart). It reflects AWS's vertical integration of custom silicon for AI economics.
words.connector: Like a factory machine built for one job — stamping out trained models — instead of a general tool, so it does that job cheaper and faster.
words.techContext: The team trains its foundation model on a cluster of Trainium-based trn2 instances to cut GPU cost.
words.exampleSentence: Switching the training run to AWS Trainium via the Neuron SDK improved cost-per-token meaningfully over GPUs.

codeExample.code:
# Launch a Trainium training instance
aws ec2 run-instances --instance-type trn1.32xlarge \
  --image-id ami-0neuron-dl --count 1

words.etymology: A blend of 'train' (model training) + the chemical-element suffix '-ium'; AWS announced it in 2020.

words.shortDefinition: Custom silicon designed to run machine-learning inference at high throughput and low cost.
words.simpleDefinition: It is an AWS-designed chip optimized for serving predictions from trained models — the inference half of ML — powering EC2 instances that aim to be cheaper per prediction than GPUs. You access it through the Neuron SDK. It is the inference counterpart to Trainium.
words.longDefinition: AWS Inferentia is a family of accelerator chips designed by AWS to deliver high-throughput, low-latency, cost-efficient machine-learning inference — the step where a trained model serves predictions in production. Inferentia powers Inf-series EC2 instances (inf1, inf2) and supports large-model and generative-AI inference at scale, accessed via the AWS Neuron SDK with PyTorch/TensorFlow integration. Compared with GPU-based inference, it targets significantly lower cost per inference and better performance-per-watt for many workloads. Inferentia and Trainium together let teams keep both training and serving on AWS-optimized silicon, improving the overall economics of running AI applications, and back services and customer deployments needing efficient, large-scale inference.
words.connector: Like a high-speed checkout lane built solely for ringing up purchases: it isn't where goods are made, but it serves customers fast and cheap.
words.techContext: The model serves from Inferentia-based inf2 instances, cutting inference cost per request versus the prior GPU fleet.
words.exampleSentence: Moving production inference to AWS Inferentia roughly halved our cost-per-prediction at the same latency.

codeExample.code:
# Launch an Inferentia inference instance
aws ec2 run-instances --instance-type inf2.xlarge \
  --image-id ami-0neuron-dl --count 1

words.etymology: A blend of 'inference' (model prediction) + the element suffix '-ia'; AWS announced it in 2018.

words.shortDefinition: A service that automatically extracts text, handwriting, forms, and tables from scanned documents.
words.simpleDefinition: It goes beyond simple OCR: it pulls out not just words but the structure — key-value form fields, table cells, and handwriting — from PDFs and images. You feed it documents and get structured data back. It is used to automate paperwork like invoices and IDs.
words.longDefinition: Amazon Textract is a machine-learning service that automatically extracts printed text, handwriting, and structured data from scanned documents and images, going beyond optical character recognition (OCR) to understand layout. It returns words and lines with bounding boxes and confidence scores, identifies key-value pairs in forms, preserves table structure, and offers specialized analyzers for common document types (invoices, receipts, identity documents, lending packages). Output is machine-readable JSON suitable for downstream automation, search, and analytics, and it integrates with Augmented AI (A2I) for human review of low-confidence results. Textract powers document-processing pipelines — accounts payable, KYC, claims, and records digitization — replacing manual data entry.
words.connector: Like a clerk who not only reads a scanned form but knows which scribble goes in which box and types it all into the spreadsheet for you.
words.techContext: Uploaded invoices hit Amazon Textract, which returns vendor, total, and line items as JSON for the AP workflow.
words.exampleSentence: Amazon Textract pulled the form fields and table rows out of the scanned PDFs so we retired manual data entry.

codeExample.code:
# Analyze a document for forms and tables
aws textract analyze-document --document '{"S3Object":{"Bucket":"docs","Name":"invoice.pdf"}}' \
  --feature-types FORMS TABLES

words.etymology: A blend of 'text' + 'extract'; AWS service launched in 2019.

words.shortDefinition: A service for analyzing images and video to detect objects, scenes, faces, text, and unsafe content.
words.simpleDefinition: It applies computer vision to your photos and videos: identifying objects and scenes, detecting and comparing faces, reading text, and flagging inappropriate content. You call an API and get labels and confidence scores back. It powers moderation, search, and identity-verification features.
words.longDefinition: Amazon Rekognition is a computer-vision service that analyzes images and video without requiring ML expertise. Capabilities include label/object and scene detection, face detection, analysis (attributes, emotions), comparison and search against a collection, text-in-image detection, content moderation (flagging unsafe or inappropriate material), celebrity recognition, personal protective equipment detection, and custom-label models trained on your own images. For video it can track people and detect activities or segments. Results carry confidence scores for thresholding. Common uses are media asset cataloging and search, content moderation at scale, identity verification, and industrial/safety inspection. Facial-analysis features are governed by AWS acceptable-use and regional considerations, so deployments must weigh privacy and compliance.
words.connector: Like an assistant with a sharp eye who can sort thousands of photos, spot who's in them, read any signs, and flag anything inappropriate — in seconds.
words.techContext: User-uploaded images pass through Amazon Rekognition content moderation before they're allowed onto the feed.
words.exampleSentence: Amazon Rekognition auto-tagged the media library by detecting objects and scenes, making assets searchable.

codeExample.code:
# Detect labels in an image stored in S3
aws rekognition detect-labels \
  --image '{"S3Object":{"Bucket":"media","Name":"photo.jpg"}}' --max-labels 10

words.etymology: A respelling of 'recognition' (to identify something known); AWS service launched in 2016.

words.shortDefinition: A service that deploys containerized web apps and APIs directly from source or an image with no infrastructure to manage.
words.simpleDefinition: You point it at a container image or a code repo, and it builds, deploys, load-balances, and autoscales your web service — including scaling to handle traffic — without you touching servers, clusters, or load balancers. It is the simplest path from code to a running, scalable web service on AWS.
words.longDefinition: AWS App Runner is a fully managed service for running containerized web applications and APIs without provisioning or managing infrastructure. You provide either a container image (from ECR) or source code (it builds the image for you), and App Runner handles deployment, TLS, load balancing, autoscaling based on concurrency, health checks, and rolling deploys. It connects to private resources via VPC connectors and integrates with observability tooling. By abstracting away clusters, load balancers, and scaling configuration, it targets developers who want a PaaS-like experience for web workloads — simpler than orchestrating ECS/EKS yourself — while still running on containers. It suits stateless HTTP services, APIs, and microservices that don't need fine-grained orchestration control.
words.connector: Like a food truck permit-and-setup service: hand over your recipe (code or image) and they park, power, and staff the truck so you just start serving.
words.techContext: The internal API ships as a container that App Runner builds, deploys, and autoscales — no ECS or load balancer to configure.
words.exampleSentence: We moved the small service off a hand-managed ECS cluster to App Runner and deleted a pile of infrastructure config.

codeExample.code:
# Create an App Runner service from a container image
aws apprunner create-service --service-name api \
  --source-configuration '{"ImageRepository":{"ImageIdentifier":"123.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/api:latest","ImageRepositoryType":"ECR"}}'

words.etymology: From 'app' (application) + 'runner' (one that runs it); AWS service launched in 2021.

words.shortDefinition: A feature that lets you run and manage container workloads on your own on-premises or other-cloud hardware using the AWS orchestrator.
words.simpleDefinition: It extends Amazon ECS to machines outside AWS — your data center or another cloud — so you register them as capacity and schedule containers on them from the same control plane. You manage on-prem containers with the same tools as in-cloud ones. It is for hybrid container deployments without running your own orchestrator.
words.longDefinition: Amazon ECS Anywhere extends the Amazon Elastic Container Service control plane to infrastructure outside AWS, letting you run and manage containers on customer-managed on-premises servers, virtual machines, or other-cloud hosts as 'external' container instances registered to an ECS cluster. The ECS agent and SSM agent on each host connect back to AWS, so you schedule, update, and observe workloads with the same ECS APIs, task definitions, and tooling used in the cloud — avoiding the need to operate a separate orchestrator like self-managed Kubernetes for hybrid estates. It suits workloads that must run near on-prem data or hardware for latency, residency, or migration reasons while keeping a unified container operations model. Pricing is a per-instance hourly fee.
words.connector: Like a head-office dispatcher who can also assign jobs to contractors' own trucks: same scheduling system, vehicles you don't own.
words.techContext: On-prem edge servers register as ECS Anywhere instances so the factory containers are scheduled from the same ECS cluster as cloud ones.
words.exampleSentence: ECS Anywhere let us keep latency-bound containers in the local data center while managing them like everything else in ECS.

codeExample.code:
# Register an external instance to an ECS cluster (run on the host)
aws ssm create-activation --iam-role ecsAnywhereRole
# then run the ECS Anywhere install script with the activation id/code

words.etymology: From the ECS service + 'Anywhere' (location-independent); launched by AWS in 2021.

words.shortDefinition: A deployment option for running Kubernetes clusters on your own on-premises infrastructure with AWS-supported tooling.
words.simpleDefinition: It lets you create and operate Kubernetes clusters in your own data center using the same distribution AWS uses, with AWS support and optional connection back to the cloud console. It is for teams that want consistent Kubernetes on-prem and in AWS. Unlike the managed EKS service, the cluster runs on your hardware.
words.longDefinition: Amazon EKS Anywhere is a deployment option that lets you create and operate Kubernetes clusters on your own on-premises infrastructure (bare metal or vSphere) using EKS Distro — the same open-source Kubernetes distribution that powers Amazon EKS. It provides opinionated cluster lifecycle tooling (creation, upgrades, scaling) and AWS support, with the option to connect clusters to the AWS console via the EKS Connector for unified visibility. Unlike the cloud EKS service (AWS manages the control plane), EKS Anywhere clusters run entirely on customer hardware, suiting data-residency, low-latency, air-gapped, or migration scenarios where a consistent, AWS-aligned Kubernetes experience on-prem is desired. It complements EKS and ECS Anywhere in the hybrid-container portfolio.
words.connector: Like building your in-house kitchen to the exact spec of the flagship restaurant's, with the same suppliers and support line on call.
words.techContext: The air-gapped site runs EKS Anywhere on bare metal so workloads use the same Kubernetes distribution as our cloud EKS clusters.
words.exampleSentence: EKS Anywhere gave the on-prem team a supported, AWS-consistent Kubernetes instead of a bespoke self-managed cluster.

codeExample.code:
# Create an EKS Anywhere cluster from a config (on the admin host)
eksctl anywhere create cluster -f eksa-cluster.yaml

words.etymology: From the EKS service + 'Anywhere' (runs off-cloud); launched by AWS in 2021.

words.shortDefinition: A feature that pre-initializes and caches a function snapshot to drastically reduce cold-start latency.
words.simpleDefinition: It takes a snapshot of your function after initialization and resumes from it on each cold start, instead of running the slow startup every time. This cuts cold-start times for runtimes with heavy init, like Java. You enable it without changing code.
words.longDefinition: AWS Lambda SnapStart reduces cold-start latency by taking an encrypted snapshot of a function's initialized execution environment (memory and disk state after the init phase) when a version is published, then resuming workers from that cached snapshot instead of re-running initialization on each cold start. Originally launched for Java (where JVM and framework startup is costly) and later extended to other runtimes like Python and .NET, it can cut cold starts from seconds to milliseconds at no extra charge for the snapshot. Developers must ensure init-time state is snapshot-safe — for example, regenerating unique values (random seeds, connections) at restore via runtime hooks — since the same snapshot is reused across environments. It targets latency-sensitive, spiky, or low-traffic functions where cold starts hurt.
words.connector: Like hibernating a laptop with all your apps already open: instead of rebooting and reloading each time, it wakes up exactly where it left off.
words.techContext: Enabling Lambda SnapStart on the Java function dropped p99 cold-start latency from ~4s to under 200ms.
words.exampleSentence: The spiky Java API felt sluggish on scale-up until Lambda SnapStart removed the worst cold starts.

codeExample.code:
# Enable SnapStart on published versions of a function
aws lambda update-function-configuration --function-name api \
  --snap-start ApplyOn=PublishedVersions

words.etymology: From 'snapshot' + 'start', describing resuming from a saved snapshot; launched by AWS in 2022.

words.shortDefinition: A feature that runs serverless functions at content-delivery edge locations to customize requests and responses near users.
words.simpleDefinition: It lets you attach Lambda functions to a CloudFront distribution so they execute at edge locations close to the viewer — rewriting requests, modifying headers, doing auth, or generating responses — without managing servers. It moves logic to the edge for lower latency. It runs on CloudFront events.
words.longDefinition: Lambda@Edge runs AWS Lambda functions at CloudFront edge locations in response to four distribution events — viewer request, origin request, origin response, and viewer response — letting you customize content delivery close to users. Common uses include request authentication and authorization, header manipulation, URL rewrites and redirects, A/B testing, bot mitigation, and generating responses at the edge to offload origins. Functions (Node.js or Python) are replicated globally by CloudFront and execute with higher resource limits and longer durations than the lighter-weight CloudFront Functions, which handle simpler, sub-millisecond viewer-event tasks. By executing logic at the edge rather than a central Region, Lambda@Edge reduces latency and origin load for globally distributed applications.
words.connector: Like having a capable clerk at every neighborhood branch who can handle your paperwork on the spot instead of mailing everything to head office.
words.techContext: A Lambda@Edge function on origin-request signs and rewrites the URL so only authorized viewers reach the private S3 origin.
words.exampleSentence: We moved auth checks to Lambda@Edge so unauthorized requests are rejected at the edge before hitting the origin.
words.etymology: From AWS 'Lambda' + '@Edge' (executing at the network edge); launched in 2017.

words.shortDefinition: Lightweight JavaScript that runs at edge locations for sub-millisecond request and response manipulation at massive scale.
words.simpleDefinition: They are tiny, ultra-fast functions that run right at CloudFront edge locations for simple tasks — header tweaks, redirects, URL rewrites, token checks — at very low cost and huge scale. They are lighter and faster than Lambda@Edge but more limited. They handle viewer request/response events only.
words.longDefinition: CloudFront Functions are short-lived, lightweight JavaScript functions that execute at CloudFront edge locations on viewer-request and viewer-response events, designed for high-scale, latency-critical, simple transformations: HTTP header manipulation, URL rewrites and redirects, cache-key normalization, simple request authorization/token validation, and A/B testing. They run in a purpose-built, highly constrained runtime with sub-millisecond startup and execution, at a fraction of the cost of Lambda@Edge, and scale to millions of requests per second. They trade capability for speed and cost — no network/file access and tight time/memory limits — so heavier logic (origin events, longer compute, external calls) belongs in Lambda@Edge. The two are complementary edge-compute options for CloudFront.
words.connector: Like a doorman who does instant, simple checks — 'is your wristband valid? go left' — far faster and cheaper than calling a full clerk for every guest.
words.techContext: A CloudFront Function normalizes the cache key and redirects HTTP to HTTPS at the edge in under a millisecond.
words.exampleSentence: For the cheap header rewrite we used a CloudFront Function instead of Lambda@Edge to save cost at our request volume.
words.etymology: Named for running 'functions' within the 'CloudFront' CDN at the edge; launched by AWS in 2021.

words.shortDefinition: A serverless, fully managed wide-column database compatible with the Apache Cassandra query language.
words.simpleDefinition: It runs Cassandra-compatible workloads without you managing any cluster: it scales automatically, charges for what you use, and speaks CQL so existing Cassandra apps and drivers work. It is for teams who want Cassandra's data model without operating Cassandra. Capacity is serverless or provisioned.
words.longDefinition: Amazon Keyspaces (for Apache Cassandra) is a serverless, fully managed, highly available wide-column database service compatible with Apache Cassandra's CQL API, drivers, and tooling. Applications connect using standard Cassandra drivers and CQL, while AWS removes cluster provisioning, patching, scaling, and repair; throughput can be on-demand (pay-per-request) or provisioned with autoscaling, and tables replicate across multiple Availability Zones with optional multi-Region replication. It targets high-scale, low-latency workloads with the Cassandra data model — time-series, IoT, messaging, and large key-value/wide-column stores — for teams that want Cassandra semantics without operating self-managed clusters. Data is encrypted at rest, integrates with IAM, and supports point-in-time recovery.
words.connector: Like getting a Cassandra database from a vending machine: same controls and queries you know, but no engine to assemble or maintain.
words.techContext: The IoT telemetry store runs on Amazon Keyspaces in on-demand mode so it scales with device bursts and we operate no cluster.
words.exampleSentence: We lifted the Cassandra app to Amazon Keyspaces unchanged and retired the self-managed ring we'd been babysitting.

codeExample.code:
-- Keyspaces speaks CQL
CREATE TABLE sensors.readings (
  device_id text, ts timestamp, value double,
  PRIMARY KEY (device_id, ts));

words.etymology: From Cassandra's term 'keyspace' (its top-level namespace, akin to a database); AWS service launched in 2020.

words.shortDefinition: A purpose-built, serverless time-series database for IoT, metrics, and other timestamped data at scale.
words.simpleDefinition: It is optimized for data points stamped with a time — sensor readings, application metrics, events — storing recent data in fast memory and older data in cheaper tiers automatically. It scales to trillions of points and has time-series query functions built in. You don't manage servers.
words.longDefinition: Amazon Timestream is a fully managed, serverless time-series database built for storing and analyzing trillions of timestamped events per day at a fraction of the cost of relational databases for this workload. Its architecture automatically tiers data between a fast in-memory store for recent data and a cost-optimized magnetic store for historical data, with configurable retention, and exposes a SQL-like query language enriched with time-series functions (interpolation, smoothing, approximation, windowing). It targets IoT telemetry, DevOps and application metrics, industrial sensors, and clickstream/analytics use cases. The newer Timestream for InfluxDB option offers compatibility with the InfluxDB ecosystem. By handling ingestion scale, tiering, and time-series analytics natively, it removes the operational burden of self-managing time-series stores.
words.connector: Like a smart logbook that keeps this week's entries on your desk and files older volumes in the cheap basement archive — but you can still search them all.
words.techContext: Device metrics stream into Amazon Timestream, which tiers last-24h data in memory and ages the rest to cheap storage.
words.exampleSentence: Querying months of sensor data got fast and cheap once we moved it from a relational table into Amazon Timestream.

codeExample.code:
-- Timestream: average value per 5-minute bin
SELECT bin(time, 5m) AS t, AVG(measure_value::double)
FROM iot.readings
WHERE time > ago(1h) GROUP BY bin(time, 5m);

words.etymology: A blend of 'time' + 'stream' (a continuous flow of data); AWS service launched in 2020.

words.shortDefinition: A fully managed graph database for storing and querying highly connected data and relationships.
words.simpleDefinition: It is built to store data as nodes and edges — people, things, and the relationships between them — and to traverse those connections fast. It supports popular graph query languages. Use it for social graphs, fraud detection, recommendations, and knowledge graphs.
words.longDefinition: Amazon Neptune is a fully managed graph database service optimized for storing billions of relationships and querying them with low latency. It supports the property-graph model (Apache TinkerPop Gremlin and openCypher query languages) and the RDF/SPARQL model for semantic/knowledge graphs, with high availability via up to 15 read replicas across Availability Zones and continuous backup to S3. Neptune suits use cases where relationships are first-class: social networking, recommendation engines, fraud detection, identity graphs, network/IT topology, and knowledge graphs. Neptune Analytics offers fast in-memory graph analytics and vector search for ML/GenAI workloads. By managing provisioning, patching, and replication, it lets teams model and traverse connected data without operating a graph engine themselves.
words.connector: Like a detective's pin-and-string board built into a database: it stores who's connected to whom and instantly traces the web of links.
words.techContext: The fraud team models accounts and transactions in Amazon Neptune and runs Gremlin traversals to spot rings of linked accounts.
words.exampleSentence: Recommendations improved once we moved the relationship data into Amazon Neptune and queried multi-hop connections directly.

codeExample.code:
# Create a Neptune cluster
aws neptune create-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier graph \
  --engine neptune

words.etymology: Named after Neptune, Roman god of the sea (and the planet), evoking depth/connection; AWS service launched in 2018.

words.shortDefinition: An on-demand mode of the cloud data warehouse that auto-scales capacity and bills only while queries run.
words.simpleDefinition: It runs the Redshift data warehouse without you provisioning or managing clusters: capacity scales automatically with workload and you pay per second of compute used, dropping to nothing when idle. It is for analytics teams who want a warehouse without capacity planning. Data and SQL are the same as provisioned Redshift.
words.longDefinition: Amazon Redshift Serverless lets you run and scale analytics on the Redshift data warehouse without provisioning or managing clusters. You define a workgroup and namespace; capacity (measured in Redshift Processing Units) scales automatically to match query demand, and you pay per second of compute consumed, with compute pausing when there's no activity. It runs the same SQL, features, and data as provisioned Redshift — including Spectrum (querying S3), federated queries, data sharing, materialized views, and ML — so workloads move between modes freely. It targets variable, unpredictable, or intermittent analytics where right-sizing a fixed cluster is wasteful, and lowers the barrier for ad-hoc and dev/test warehousing. Provisioned clusters remain preferable for steady, high-utilization workloads where reserved pricing wins.
words.connector: Like a banquet hall that expands and contracts with the crowd and only charges for the chairs actually used, then folds away when everyone leaves.
words.techContext: The BI workload runs on Redshift Serverless so capacity scales for morning dashboard spikes and costs nothing overnight.
words.exampleSentence: We dropped the always-on cluster for Redshift Serverless and our warehouse bill now tracks actual query usage.

codeExample.code:
# Create a serverless namespace and workgroup
aws redshift-serverless create-namespace --namespace-name analytics
aws redshift-serverless create-workgroup --workgroup-name bi \
  --namespace-name analytics

words.etymology: From the 'Redshift' warehouse + 'serverless' (no managed servers); the mode launched in 2021.

words.shortDefinition: A managed service for running search and log-analytics workloads on the OpenSearch and Elasticsearch engines.
words.simpleDefinition: It runs OpenSearch (the open-source fork of Elasticsearch) for you — provisioning, scaling, patching, and backing up clusters — so you can do full-text search, log analytics, and observability with dashboards. A serverless option removes capacity management. It also supports vector search for AI applications.
words.longDefinition: Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed service for deploying, operating, and scaling OpenSearch (and legacy Elasticsearch) clusters for search and analytics. It handles provisioning, patching, scaling, snapshots, and high availability across Availability Zones, and bundles OpenSearch Dashboards for visualization, plus features for log analytics, full-text and faceted search, observability/SIEM, and k-NN vector search for semantic and GenAI retrieval. OpenSearch Serverless offers an option without cluster sizing, auto-scaling compute and storage for indexing and search collections. It integrates with ingestion pipelines (OpenSearch Ingestion, Kinesis, Firehose) and IAM/fine-grained access control. It targets log/observability platforms, application and website search, and increasingly vector-based AI search, removing the operational burden of self-managing the engine.
words.connector: Like hiring a librarian and the whole library system: instant lookups across millions of documents, with someone else keeping the shelves and catalog running.
words.techContext: Application and access logs ship to Amazon OpenSearch Service, where dashboards and alerting drive our observability.
words.exampleSentence: We added semantic search to the app using the k-NN vector feature of Amazon OpenSearch Service.

codeExample.code:
# Create a managed OpenSearch domain
aws opensearch create-domain --domain-name logs \
  --engine-version OpenSearch_2.13 \
  --cluster-config InstanceType=r6g.large.search,InstanceCount=3

words.etymology: From the open-source 'OpenSearch' project (an Elasticsearch fork AWS created in 2021).

words.shortDefinition: A data-management service to catalog, govern, share, and discover data across an organization.
words.simpleDefinition: It provides a business-friendly catalog and portal where teams publish data assets, others discover and request access, and governance is enforced through approval workflows. It connects producers and consumers of data across accounts. It is about data discovery and governance, not storage.
words.longDefinition: Amazon DataZone is a data-management service that helps organizations catalog, discover, share, and govern data at scale across accounts, on-prem, and third-party sources. It provides a web portal (the business data catalog) where data producers publish assets enriched with business metadata (often auto-generated with ML/GenAI), and consumers search a glossary-driven catalog, then request and receive governed access through approval workflows. Concepts like domains, projects, and environments organize teams and their analytics resources (integrating with Glue, Redshift, Athena, and SageMaker), while access policies and audit trails enforce governance. DataZone bridges the gap between data platform teams and business users, reducing the friction of finding trustworthy data and the risk of ungoverned sharing. It evolves toward the broader SageMaker data-and-AI governance experience.
words.connector: Like an internal app store for data: teams list their datasets with descriptions, others browse and request access, and an approval gate keeps it governed.
words.techContext: Analysts find and request governed access to the sales dataset through the Amazon DataZone portal instead of emailing the data team.
words.exampleSentence: Amazon DataZone cut data-discovery time because every certified dataset is searchable with business context in one catalog.

codeExample.code:
# List DataZone domains
aws datazone list-domains \
  --query 'items[].{Name:name,Id:id,Status:status}'

words.etymology: From 'data' + 'zone' (a governed area); AWS service launched in 2023.

words.shortDefinition: A service that lets multiple parties analyze combined datasets together without sharing or exposing the underlying raw data.
words.simpleDefinition: It creates a secure, governed space where companies can run agreed-upon queries across each other's data and see only aggregated results, never the raw rows. Each party keeps control of its own data. It is built for privacy-preserving collaboration, like advertising measurement.
words.longDefinition: AWS Clean Rooms enables multiple parties to collaborate on and analyze their collective datasets without sharing or copying one another's underlying raw data. Each participant brings data (kept in their own S3/Glue) into a configured collaboration with agreed analysis rules; only permitted aggregate queries run, governed by analysis rules, query controls, and privacy-enhancing techniques including differential privacy and cryptographic computing (Clean Rooms ML for lookalike modeling without sharing data). It is widely used for advertising and marketing measurement, audience overlap, and any cross-company analytics where regulation or competition forbids exchanging raw records. By enforcing that participants see only sanctioned outputs, it lets organizations derive joint insights while preserving data privacy and ownership.
words.connector: Like two companies meeting in a sealed room with a neutral analyst: they get the combined report they agreed on, but neither walks out with the other's files.
words.techContext: The advertiser and publisher measure campaign overlap in AWS Clean Rooms, seeing only aggregate results, never each other's user lists.
words.exampleSentence: AWS Clean Rooms let the two firms compute audience overlap without either ever exposing its raw customer data.

codeExample.code:
# List clean-room collaborations you're a member of
aws cleanrooms list-collaborations \
  --query 'collaborationList[].{Name:name,Id:id}'

words.etymology: From 'clean room' (a contamination-controlled space), here for data isolation; AWS service launched in 2023.

words.shortDefinition: A managed service for running controlled chaos-engineering experiments to test how systems withstand failure.
words.simpleDefinition: It deliberately injects faults — like terminating instances, adding latency, or throttling APIs — under controlled conditions so you can verify your application actually survives real failures. You define experiments with guardrails that stop them if things go too far. It turns disaster recovery from theory into tested fact.
words.longDefinition: AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) is a managed chaos-engineering service that runs controlled fault-injection experiments to reveal how applications respond to real-world failures and to validate resilience assumptions. You define experiment templates specifying actions (e.g., stop/terminate EC2 instances, inject CPU/memory/IO stress, add network latency or packet loss, throttle API calls, fail over RDS/Aurora, or simulate an Availability Zone or cross-Region impairment) against tagged targets, with stop conditions tied to CloudWatch alarms that automatically halt the experiment if blast radius exceeds safe bounds. FIS integrates with monitoring so you observe behavior and verify recovery, supporting practices like game days and continuous resilience testing. It operationalizes chaos engineering safely, complementing Resilience Hub's assessment of recovery objectives.
words.connector: Like a fire drill you schedule on purpose, with a supervisor ready to call it off the instant anyone is in real danger.
words.techContext: A monthly Fault Injection Service experiment kills an Availability Zone's instances to prove the service stays up, with a CloudWatch alarm as the abort switch.
words.exampleSentence: The Fault Injection Service game day exposed that our failover took 4 minutes, not the 30 seconds we'd assumed.

codeExample.code:
# Start a predefined FIS experiment
aws fis start-experiment --experiment-template-id EXT123abc

words.etymology: Descriptive: a service that performs 'fault injection', a long-standing reliability-testing technique; launched 2021.

words.shortDefinition: A service that assesses an application's resilience against recovery targets and recommends improvements.
words.simpleDefinition: It evaluates whether your application can meet its recovery-time and recovery-point goals, scores its resilience, and suggests fixes and tests. It tracks resilience over time as you change the system. It works alongside chaos testing to validate disaster recovery.
words.longDefinition: AWS Resilience Hub provides a central place to define, assess, and track the resilience of applications against your recovery objectives — Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO). You describe an application (often imported from CloudFormation, Resource Groups, or AppRegistry), set target RTO/RPO per disruption type (infrastructure, AZ, or Region failure), and Resilience Hub analyzes the architecture to estimate whether targets are met, surfacing gaps and concrete recommendations (e.g., enable Multi-AZ, add backups, adjust replication). It can generate operational recommendations (alarms, SOPs) and integrates with Fault Injection Service to validate findings through experiments, tracking a resilience score over time. It turns resilience from an assumption into a measured, continuously evaluated property.
words.connector: Like a building inspector for disaster-readiness: they check whether you can actually evacuate and rebuild in the time you promised, and list what to fix.
words.techContext: Resilience Hub flagged that the app couldn't meet its 1-minute RPO because one table lacked cross-Region replication.
words.exampleSentence: Resilience Hub scored the service against our RTO/RPO targets and recommended the Multi-AZ changes we'd overlooked.

codeExample.code:
# List applications tracked in Resilience Hub
aws resiliencehub list-apps \
  --query 'appSummaries[].{Name:name,Compliance:complianceStatus}'

words.etymology: From 'resilience' (ability to recover) + 'hub' (a central point); AWS service launched in 2021.

words.shortDefinition: A managed service for centralized, fine-grained authorization in your own applications using a dedicated policy language.
words.simpleDefinition: It externalizes your app's authorization logic: instead of scattering 'can this user do this?' checks through code, you write policies in the Cedar language and ask the service for a decision. It scales permission management and makes it auditable. It is for end-user/app authorization, not AWS IAM.
words.longDefinition: Amazon Verified Permissions is a scalable, fine-grained authorization service for custom applications, built on the open-source Cedar policy language. Rather than embedding authorization logic throughout application code, developers define who can do what on which resources as Cedar policies in a central policy store, then call the service's IsAuthorized API at request time to get an allow/deny decision based on the principal, action, resource, and contextual attributes (ABAC and RBAC). This centralizes and standardizes permissions, makes them auditable and testable, and lets policy change without redeploying code. It integrates with identity providers (including Cognito) and suits multi-tenant SaaS and any app needing rich, maintainable end-user authorization — distinct from IAM, which authorizes calls to AWS itself.
words.connector: Like moving every 'who's allowed in?' rule out of scattered sticky notes into one official rulebook the bouncer consults for each request.
words.techContext: The SaaS app calls Verified Permissions with the user, action, and resource, and enforces the Cedar policy decision it returns.
words.exampleSentence: Centralizing authorization in Verified Permissions let us change a sharing rule via policy without shipping new code.

codeExample.code:
# Ask Verified Permissions for an authorization decision
aws verifiedpermissions is-authorized --policy-store-id PS123 \
  --principal '{"entityType":"User","entityId":"alice"}' \
  --action '{"actionType":"Action","actionId":"viewDoc"}'

words.etymology: From 'verified' (checked/proven) + 'permissions' (authorizations); AWS service launched in 2023.

words.shortDefinition: A serverless, distributed SQL database offering active-active multi-Region operation with strong consistency and PostgreSQL compatibility.
words.simpleDefinition: It is a newer database that runs across multiple Regions active-active — every Region accepts reads and writes with strong consistency — while being serverless and PostgreSQL-compatible, with virtually unlimited scale and no servers to manage. It targets the hardest globally-distributed, always-on workloads. It removes the usual trade-off between global scale and SQL consistency.
words.longDefinition: Amazon Aurora DSQL is a serverless, distributed SQL database engineered for high availability and scale with PostgreSQL compatibility. It offers active-active multi-Region deployments where all endpoints accept reads and writes with strong consistency, automatic scaling of compute and storage with no instances to provision or patch, and a design that decouples transaction processing from storage to scale horizontally. It targets demanding, globally distributed OLTP applications that need both relational/SQL semantics and resilience to Region-level failure without the complexity of sharding or manual replication. As AWS's distributed-SQL offering, it advances beyond classic Aurora (single-writer, regional) toward a multi-writer, multi-Region model, trading some of PostgreSQL's surface area for distributed guarantees and operational simplicity.
words.connector: Like a single ledger magically kept identical and authoritative in offices on three continents, where anyone can write and everyone instantly agrees.
words.techContext: The global app writes to Aurora DSQL in whichever Region the user hits, with strong consistency across all of them and no failover step.
words.exampleSentence: Aurora DSQL let us run active-active across two Regions without building our own conflict-resolution layer.

codeExample.code:
# Create an Aurora DSQL cluster (preview/GA CLI)
aws dsql create-cluster --no-deletion-protection-enabled \
  --query 'identifier'

words.etymology: From the 'Aurora' database brand + 'DSQL' (Distributed SQL); previewed by AWS in late 2024.
